item.text: I’m pulling the RFC text directly and will answer from that source only unless I need a second authoritative copy for clarity.

**Supported Fact**

Under RFC 9309, a `robots.txt` *group* is one or more `user-agent` lines followed by one or more rules, and the group ends when another `user-agent` line appears or the file ends. The last group may have no rules, which means it implicitly allows everything. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309.txt

For user-agent matching, crawlers must use **case-insensitive** matching against their product token. If more than one group matches the same user-agent, the crawler must **combine** those groups’ rules into one group and then parse that merged set of rules. If no specific group matches, the crawler must use the `user-agent: *` group if one exists. If neither a specific match nor `*` exists, then **no rules apply**. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309.txt

For `allow`/`disallow` precedence, the crawler must compare the URI against the group’s rules starting from the **first octet** of the path, and the **most specific** match wins; RFC 9309 defines “most specific” as the match with the **most octets**. If an `allow` rule and a `disallow` rule are equivalent, the `allow` rule **should** be used. If no rule matches, or the matching group has no rules, the URI is allowed. The `/robots.txt` URI itself is implicitly allowed. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309.txt

For percent encoding, octets in the URI and in `robots.txt` paths that are outside ASCII, and octets in the RFC 3986 reserved range, must be **percent-encoded before comparison**. If the URI contains a percent-encoded ASCII octet, the crawler must **decode** it before comparison, unless that octet is a reserved URI character or is outside the unreserved range. A match succeeds only if the rule path ends before any differing octet is encountered. RFC 9309 also says crawlers should percent-encode literal special characters when matching them verbatim in a URI. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309.txt

For an **unavailable** `robots.txt`, RFC 9309 defines that as the crawler attempting to fetch `/robots.txt` and receiving a response indicating the resource is unavailable; in HTTP, the RFC gives **400-499** as the example range. In that case, the crawler **may access any resources on the server**. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309.txt

RFC 9309 separately defines **unreachable** `robots.txt` as server or network errors; in HTTP, it gives **500-599** as the example range. In that case, the crawler must assume **complete disallow**. If that undefined state lasts for a reasonably long time, with **30 days** given as an example, the crawler may then treat it as unavailable or keep using a cached copy. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309.txt

**Inference**

A practical reading is that RFC 9309 resolves `allow` vs `disallow` conflicts primarily by **longest-path match**, not by a blanket “allow always beats disallow” rule; `allow` only gets tie-breaking preference when the two rules are equivalent in specificity. This is an inference from the RFC’s ordering rules, not a separately stated summary sentence. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309.txt

A practical reading is also that “unavailable” means **permission to crawl by default**, while “unreachable” means **deny by default**, because the RFC assigns those opposite outcomes to the two conditions. This is an inference from the RFC’s normative handling rules. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309.txt

**Disagreement / Uncertainty**

I found no disagreement inside RFC 9309 itself on these four points. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309.txt

There is mild implementation uncertainty at the ecosystem level because RFC 9309 uses both **MUST** and **SHOULD** language in different places, so behavior such as case-sensitive path matching or tie handling can be stricter or looser depending on the implementation. That uncertainty is about real-world conformance, not about what the RFC text says. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309.txt

**Lack of Good Evidence**

I do not have good evidence, from RFC 9309 alone, to claim how any specific crawler actually behaves in production beyond what the RFC requires or recommends. RFC 9309 is the specification; it is not an implementation survey. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309.txt
